sections.title: What a program actually does
sections.text: A program is a sequence of instructions applied to data. Python executes a file from top to bottom. A function definition stores a reusable set of instructions; its body runs when the function is called. The browser checks call your function with different inputs. They do not read your intentions, so the function name, arguments, and returned value must match the task.

sections.title: Values, names, and expressions
sections.text: An integer such as 8 is a whole-number value; a float such as 8.5 represents a fractional number; a string such as "8" is text. True and False are booleans. None represents an explicitly absent result. An expression produces a value: 8 + 2 produces 10. Assignment such as coins = 8 binds a name to a value. Later coins = coins + 2 reads the old value, computes the sum, and updates the binding. Assignment uses =; equality comparison uses ==.

sections.title: Syntax you need before the first challenge
sections.text: def starts a function definition. Parameters in parentheses name the inputs. A colon starts the indented body, conventionally four spaces. return gives a result back to the caller and exits the function. print displays text for a person; a function that only prints returns None. A # starts a comment and pass is a placeholder that does nothing. Python is case-sensitive, so Total and total are different names.

sections.title: Arithmetic and decisions
sections.text: Use +, -, *, and / for arithmetic; / produces a float. // is floor division and % is the remainder. Parentheses control grouping. Compare with <, <=, >, >=, ==, and !=. and requires both conditions, or requires at least one, and not reverses a boolean. An if/elif/else chain chooses a branch. Test exactly at each cutoff as well as on either side. Strings and numeric values do not combine automatically; convert deliberately with int(), float(), or str().

worked.code:
def remaining(coins, price):
    if coins < price:
        return None
    return coins - price

print(remaining(12, 5))
print(remaining(5, 5))
print(remaining(4, 5))
trace: The first call binds coins to 12 and price to 5. The comparison is False, so the final return gives 7.
At equal amounts the purchase is allowed, returning 0. An insufficient amount takes the early return.
print displays each returned value. Removing print would still compute values but a script would not display them.

mistakes: Using = instead of == in a condition.
Printing the answer instead of returning it.
Indenting return under the wrong branch or misspelling a parameter.
questions: Why is "12" + "5" different from 12 + 5?
What does a function return when it reaches its end with no return?
Which three inputs test the cutoff at price 5?

units.title: Start small
units.prerequisites: Start Here and basic computer file operations

plain.title: What you are actually doing
plain.text:
A program is a list of instructions that the computer follows from top to bottom, exactly as written. It never guesses what you meant. That sounds harsh, but it's also what makes programming learnable: when something goes wrong, there is always a concrete reason, and you can find it by reading carefully.

In Forge, almost every challenge asks you to write a function: a named, reusable recipe. You give it inputs, it does some work, and it hands back one result.
plain.code:
def add_xp(current, earned):   # a recipe named add_xp with two inputs
    total = current + earned    # do the work
    return total                # hand the result back

add_xp(20, 15)   # calling the recipe gives back 35

plain.title: Variables are labels, not boxes
plain.text:
total = current + earned does two things. First Python works out the right-hand side (20 + 15 = 35). Then it sticks the label total onto that value. If you later write total = total + 1, Python computes 36 and moves the label to the new value.

Read = as 'now refers to', never as 'equals'. That one habit prevents a lot of confusion. To compare two values, use == instead.
plain.code:
hp = 30
hp = hp - 12     # right side first: 30 - 12 = 18, then hp refers to 18
print(hp == 18)  # True: == compares, = assigns

plain.title: return vs print
plain.text: This trips up nearly every beginner. print shows text on the screen for a human to read. return sends a value back to whoever called the function, so other code can use it. Forge's checks call your function and look at what it returns. If you print the answer instead, the function returns None and the check fails, even though you can see the right number on screen.

plain.title: Making decisions
plain.text:
if lets a program choose. The condition after if is checked; if it's True, the indented block runs. elif means 'otherwise, if', and else catches everything left over. Python uses indentation (four spaces) to know which lines belong to which block, so indentation is not decoration: it changes the meaning.

When a function returns inside an if, it stops right there. That's why you can check the most extreme case first and let later checks handle what remains.

plain.title: How to attack any challenge
plain.text:
1. Read the task twice and write down the inputs and the output.
2. Work two examples by hand, including an edge case such as 0, an empty list, or the exact boundary value.
3. Write the function. Keep it boring and obvious.
4. Run the checks. If one fails, read its input, expected value, and received value, then trace your code line by line with that exact input.

The tracing in step 4 is the skill you're building. It's what lets you check AI-written code later instead of trusting it blindly.

plain.title: Values have types
plain.text:
Every value has a type, and the type decides what you can do with it. 7 is an int (a whole number). 7.5 is a float (a number with a decimal point). "7" is a str (text), even though it looks like a number. True and False are bools.

Mixing them is the first error most people hit. "7" + 1 fails because Python won't guess whether you meant text or maths. Convert on purpose with int(), float(), or str(). When you're unsure, type() tells you what you have.
plain.code:
print(type(7), type(7.5), type("7"), type(True))
print(int("7") + 1)      # 8
print("7" + str(1))      # 71: joining text, not adding
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2)   # 3.5 3 1: divide, whole divide, remainder

plain.title: Text, and building it with f-strings
plain.text:
Text goes in quotes. len() counts its characters, and methods like .lower() and .strip() return a cleaned-up copy without changing the original.

To put values inside text, use an f-string: put f before the quote and any expression inside { }. It's clearer than gluing pieces together with +, and it converts numbers for you.
plain.code:
name = "  Ada "
clean = name.strip()
hp = 30
print(len(clean))
print(f"{clean} has {hp} HP")
print(f"Half of that is {hp / 2}")

sections.title: Lists and positions
sections.text: A list is an ordered collection: [3, 7, 2]. Its first index is 0, so values[0] is 3. A negative index counts from the end; values[-1] is 2. values[1:3] slices from index 1 up to, but excluding, index 3. len(values) gives its length. Indexing an empty list raises IndexError. Lists can change: append adds an element and pop removes one. Strings support indexing and slicing too, but cannot be changed in place.

sections.title: Loops and accumulators
sections.text: for item in values binds item to each value in sequence. range(3) produces 0, 1, 2; range(1, 4) produces 1, 2, 3. Use enumerate(values) when you need both index and item. An accumulator starts before the loop, updates inside it, and is returned after it. A misplaced return inside the loop stops after the first item. A while loop repeats while a condition holds; update the state so it can eventually stop.

sections.title: Filter and transform
sections.text: Filtering keeps selected items; mapping changes each item. Start with explicit loops so you can trace their behavior. Later, [x * 2 for x in values if x > 0] combines filtering and mapping in a comprehension. It builds a new list. A generator expression uses parentheses instead: (x * 2 for x in values) produces results one at a time when consumed. sum totals numbers, any returns whether at least one value is truthy, and all returns whether every value is truthy. For empty input, sum returns 0 by default, any returns False, and all returns True. Trace the equivalent loop before using the compact form. Do not remove items from the collection you are iterating unless you fully understand the consequences. A fresh result list makes the contract easier to reason about.

sections.title: Strings and boundaries
sections.text: strip removes whitespace from both ends, lower changes case, replace substitutes occurrences, split divides text, and join combines strings using a separator. These methods return new values. An f-string such as f"Score: {score}" formats a value into text. Decide whether repeated internal spaces should remain or collapse. A normalization function must reflect the spec, not your guess about what a clean name should look like.

trace: Start total at 0. Read 4 and add it, so total becomes 4.
Read -2; the condition fails and the accumulator stays 4. Read 3 and add it to get 7.
The return happens after the loop. An empty list never enters the loop, so its result is the initial 0.

mistakes: Resetting the accumulator inside the loop.
Returning after the first iteration.
Using a list index before checking that the list contains an item.
questions: What does range(2, 5) produce?

units.title: Make it repeatable

plain.title: Lists hold things in order
plain.text: A list is an ordered collection: [3, 8, 1]. Positions (indexes) start at 0, so the first item is scores[0] and the last is scores[-1]. len(scores) tells you how many items there are. Lists can grow with .append(value).
plain.code:
scores = [3, 8, 1]
print(scores[0])    # 3
print(scores[-1])   # 1
scores.append(10)
print(len(scores))  # 4

plain.title: A loop does the same thing for each item
plain.text: for item in collection: runs the indented block once per item, with item referring to a different element each time. The most important loop pattern is the accumulator: make a variable before the loop, update it inside, and use it after.
plain.code:
def total_damage(hits):
    total = 0              # 1. start before the loop
    for hit in hits:
        total += hit       # 2. update for each item
    return total           # 3. use it after the loop

# Trace with [4, 6]:
#   total = 0
#   hit = 4 -> total = 4
#   hit = 6 -> total = 10
#   return 10

plain.title: Tracing: your most important skill
plain.text:
When a loop gives the wrong answer, don't change things at random. Take the smallest input that fails, and write down every variable after every line, like the trace above. The moment your written trace disagrees with what you expected, you've found the bug. It feels slow at first. It becomes fast, and it's the core of debugging.

A common bug: putting return inside the loop. That returns after the first item, because return always ends the function immediately.

plain.title: Building a new list
plain.text: To filter or transform, start with an empty list and append what you want to keep. Python also has a shorthand called a list comprehension. Learn the long form first; the short form is the same thing written compactly.

plain.title: Strings are sequences too
plain.text: A string is a sequence of characters, so you can loop over it, index it, and slice it. Strings never change in place: methods like .strip(), .lower(), and .replace() return a new string, so you must keep the result.
plain.code:
name = "  Dark Souls "
name.strip()               # returns "Dark Souls" but name is unchanged!
name = name.strip()        # keep the result
print(name.lower().replace(" ", "_"))   # dark_souls

plain.title: zip and enumerate
plain.text:
Two tools replace most manual index counting. enumerate gives you each item with its position. zip walks two lists side by side and stops at the shorter one.

If you catch yourself writing for i in range(len(items)), one of these is usually cleaner.

plain.title: A loop inside a loop
plain.text: A nested loop runs the whole inner loop once for every pass of the outer loop. It's how you visit every pair of things, or every cell of a grid. Trace it slowly the first few times: the inner variable resets on each outer pass.

goals: Choose a list, tuple, dictionary, or set for a reason.

sections.title: Choose by operation
sections.text: A list preserves order and duplicates. A tuple is an immutable sequence, useful for a fixed pair such as (x, y). A dictionary maps unique keys to values and preserves insertion order. A set stores unique hashable values for membership tests; do not depend on its iteration order for a report. Strings, numbers, and tuples of hashable values can be keys; mutable lists cannot. Choose based on what you need to do, not which syntax looks shortest. For sets, a | b is union, a & b is intersection, and a - b is difference. These operations also work with dictionary key views. A membership test uses in; use not in for its opposite.

sections.title: Count and look up
sections.text: counts[item] raises KeyError if the key is missing. counts.get(item, 0) supplies a starting value without inserting it. Updating counts[item] = counts.get(item, 0) + 1 accumulates a frequency. Use key in mapping to distinguish a missing key from a stored value of None or 0. mapping.items() yields key/value pairs that can be unpacked in a loop.

sections.title: Objects and copies
sections.text: Assignment does not copy a collection: b = a makes both names refer to the same list. Modifying b can therefore change what a sees. a.copy() makes a shallow top-level copy; nested collections are still shared. A pure transformation returns a new result and leaves the caller’s input alone. You will need this distinction whenever a task says do not mutate.

sections.title: Sorting is a policy
sections.text: sorted(values) returns a new ordered list; list.sort() changes the list and returns None. key chooses a comparison value. lambda record: record["score"] is a tiny function returning a score. A tuple key such as (-score, name) means score descending, then name ascending. Stable sorting retains original order when keys compare equally. Define ties explicitly rather than relying on accidental order.

gem starts at 1. The second coin reads the existing count 1 and updates it to 2.
The function returns a dictionary; the loop did not need to scan prior items to count the current item.

mistakes: Assuming a set preserves the report order you need.

units.title: Think in collections

plain.title: Dictionaries: look things up by name
plain.text: A list finds things by position. A dictionary finds things by key. Think of a dictionary as a two-column table: keys on the left, values on the right. Keys are unique; assigning to an existing key replaces its value.
plain.code:
inventory = {"potion": 2, "key": 1}
print(inventory["potion"])      # 2
inventory["potion"] = 3         # replace
inventory["sword"] = 1          # add a new key
print("bow" in inventory)       # False: checks keys

plain.title: The counting pattern
plain.text: Counting how often things appear is one of the most common tasks in real code. Use .get(key, 0): it returns the current count, or 0 if the key isn't there yet.

plain.title: Sets: unique values, fast membership
plain.text: A set holds each value once and answers 'have I seen this?' very quickly. Use it to remove duplicates or to track what you've already handled. Sets have no order, so sort the result if order matters.

plain.title: Copies vs. the same object
plain.text: b = a does not copy a list or dictionary. Both names now point at the same object, so changing one changes 'both'. When a task says 'do not mutate', make a copy first. This bug is subtle and very common in real codebases.
plain.code:
a = {"hp": 10}
b = a           # same dictionary, two names
b["hp"] = 0
print(a)        # {'hp': 0}  surprise!

c = dict(a)     # a real (shallow) copy
c["hp"] = 99
print(a)        # {'hp': 0}  unchanged

plain.title: Sorting with a key
plain.text: sorted(items, key=...) sorts by whatever the key function returns. A tuple key sorts by the first part, then the second to break ties. Negating a number flips it to descending without reversing the tie-breaker.
plain.code:
players = [{"name": "bo", "score": 5}, {"name": "ana", "score": 5}, {"name": "cy", "score": 9}]
ordered = sorted(players, key=lambda p: (-p["score"], p["name"]))
print([p["name"] for p in ordered])   # ['cy', 'ana', 'bo']

plain.title: Data inside data
plain.text:
Real data nests: lists of dictionaries, dictionaries of lists, dictionaries inside dictionaries. Nothing new is happening. Each [ ] reads one level, left to right, and every step gives you a value you can index again.

When it feels confusing, print one level at a time and see what you've got.
plain.code:
players = [
    {"name": "Ada", "scores": [10, 40]},
    {"name": "Bo", "scores": [25]},
]
print(players[0]["name"])        # Ada
print(players[0]["scores"][1])   # 40
for p in players:
    print(p["name"], max(p["scores"]))

sections.title: State and transitions
sections.text: State is the information needed to describe the current game: position, health, inventory, and turn. A transition takes state plus a command and produces the next state. Keeping this calculation separate from rendering and keyboard input makes it possible to test a game without graphics. Begin with the smallest playable rule rather than an entire game engine.

sections.title: Unpacking and movement
sections.text: A position can be a tuple or list of two numbers. dx, dy = (1, 0) unpacks two values into two names. A command mapping turns a direction into a movement vector. Unknown commands need an explicit policy: ignore them, reject them, or return an error. In a bounded map, define whether invalid movement stays put or clamps to an edge.

sections.title: Termination and invariants
sections.text: A while loop needs progress. If each attack subtracts positive damage, health eventually reaches the stopping condition. Zero damage requires a separate rule because no progress occurs. An invariant is a condition that remains true after each transition, such as health >= 0. Use max(0, value) to enforce a lower bound when it matches the game rules.

sections.title: Modules and simple tests
sections.text: A module is a .py file containing reusable definitions. from core import move loads a function from core.py. Keep the executable application under if __name__ == "__main__": so importing the module does not start the game. A basic assertion such as assert move(0, 0, "N") == [0, 1] is an executable expectation. Separate core.py, main.py, and test_core.py once a single file becomes hard to navigate.

trace: The first transition reduces health from 5 to 3.

Printing is outside next_health; the function can be tested without any display.

mistakes: Putting rendering, input, and state changes in one hard-to-test function.
Running a combat loop when damage can be zero.
Changing the rules while debugging instead of checking the written spec.

units.title: Build a game engine

plain.title: State is just variables over time
plain.text:
A game is a loop that repeatedly reads input, updates state (position, health, score), and shows the result. You already have every tool for this: variables for state, if for rules, and loops for repetition. This week is about combining them without getting lost.

Write the state down explicitly. Ask, for every rule: what is the state before, what input arrives, and what is the state after?

plain.title: Clamping and invariants
plain.text: An invariant is a rule that must always stay true, such as 'health is never negative'. Enforce it every time state changes. max(0, value) keeps a value from going below 0; min(limit, value) keeps it from going above a limit.
plain.code:
hp, max_hp, damage, heal = 5, 30, 8, 50
hp = max(0, hp - damage)        # never below 0
hp = min(max_hp, hp + heal)     # never above max_hp

plain.title: while loops need an exit
plain.text: for loops over a collection always end. while loops keep going as long as a condition is True, so something inside must eventually make it False. If a run hits Forge's time limit, an infinite loop is the usual cause: check that every path changes the loop variable.
plain.code:
hp, damage = 10, 3
turns = 0
while hp > 0:
    hp -= damage    # this line is what eventually ends the loop
    turns += 1

plain.title: Splitting code into functions
plain.text: When one function gets long, pull a piece out into its own named function: move(x, y, cmd) inside dungeon(commands). Small functions are easier to test, name, and explain in an interview. A good rule: if you can't describe what a function does in one sentence, it's doing too much.

sections.title: Three kinds of failure
sections.text: A syntax error prevents Python from parsing the program. A runtime exception happens during execution, such as accessing a missing key. A logic bug runs but produces the wrong answer. Use different evidence for each: a parser location, a traceback, or an expected/actual comparison. A red test is a starting point for investigation.

sections.title: Tracebacks and debugging
sections.text: Read the exception type and message at the end, then find the last relevant line in your own code. Reproduce the smallest failing input. Check variable values with a temporary print or a debugger breakpoint. Form one hypothesis and test it. When you fix the bug, preserve the input as a regression test so it does not quietly return.

sections.title: Exceptions and validation
sections.text: try protects code that might raise an expected exception; except ValueError handles that type. Do not put your entire program in except Exception and report success. int("4") succeeds, int("four") fails, and int("4.5") also fails. None can represent an invalid parsed result, but callers must handle it before arithmetic. Check types before calling methods or comparing missing values.

sections.title: Truth is not presence
sections.text: An empty list, empty string, zero, False, and None are falsy in conditions. They do not mean the same thing. if not scores is useful for rejecting an empty list, but if value may be 0, use an explicit check such as value is None. Short-circuit conditions help validate safely: check isinstance(name, str) before name.strip(). Avoid dividing by len(values) until you know the list is nonempty.

trace: The first conversion succeeds and zero passes the nonnegative rule.
The second conversion raises ValueError, handled by the specific except.
A caller must distinguish a legitimate count 0 from the invalid marker None.

mistakes: Catching every exception and hiding unrelated bugs.
Treating zero as missing.
Changing several things at once without a reproducible example.
questions: Is the failure syntax, runtime, or logic?
Why is if value is None different from if not value?

plain.title: Three kinds of errors
plain.text: A SyntaxError means Python can't even read your code (a missing colon or bracket). A runtime error (ValueError, KeyError, TypeError, ZeroDivisionError…) happens while the code runs. A logic error is the sneakiest: no crash, just a wrong answer. The checks catch logic errors; tracing finds them.

plain.title: Reading a traceback
plain.text: When Python crashes it prints a traceback. Read it from the bottom up. The last line names the error and gives a message. The line above it shows where it happened in your file. That's usually enough to find the problem.
plain.code:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "solution.py", line 3, in average_score
    return sum(scores) / len(scores)
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

# Bottom line: dividing by zero.
# Line 3: len(scores) was 0, so the list was empty.
# Fix: handle the empty list before dividing.

plain.title: try / except: expecting failure
plain.text: Some failures are normal, such as a user typing 'abc' where a number belongs. try runs code that might fail; except catches a specific error and lets you respond. Always name the error you expect (except ValueError:). A bare except: hides real bugs too.

plain.title: Validate early
plain.text:
Check bad input at the top of the function and return early. Then the rest of the function can assume clean data. This guard-clause style is easier to read than deeply nested if/else blocks.

Watch out for truthiness: 0, "", [], and None all count as False in an if. 'if not value' can reject a legitimate 0. When 0 is valid, check explicitly: 'if value is None'.

plain.title: Raising your own errors
plain.text:
So far you've caught errors that Python raises. You can raise them too. When a function gets something it can't work with, raise stops it immediately and hands the problem to the caller.

This beats returning a strange value like -1, which a caller can forget to check. Exceptions can't be ignored by accident: they keep travelling up until something catches them.

sections.title: Files and resources
sections.text: A file handle is a resource. with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8") as handle closes it when the block exits, including on an exception. Read mode does not create a missing file; write mode can overwrite existing content. Use a dedicated practice folder. The browser’s Python filesystem is temporary and separate from your computer, so real persistent file labs run locally.

sections.title: JSON is a format, not a Python expression
sections.text: json.loads reads JSON text into Python objects; json.dumps produces text. File-based json.load and json.dump use handles. JSON null maps to None and true/false map to Python booleans. Parsing successfully does not prove the result has the shape your application needs. Check that expected lists, keys, and value types are present before processing.

sections.title: CSV and text streams
sections.text: csv.DictReader reads headers into dictionary keys. Most CSV field values arrive as strings, so convert numeric fields deliberately. A quoted title may contain a comma; split(",") cannot reliably parse it. io.StringIO lets the same parser read an in-memory string for tests. Use newline="" when opening real CSV files and let csv handle delimiters and quoting.

sections.title: Paths and pure processing
sections.text: pathlib represents paths and their components. PurePosixPath computes components without touching a disk; Path can access the local filesystem. A suffix is not proof of valid file contents. Design a core that transforms records, then write a thin wrapper to read and write files. This prevents tests from needing a real filesystem for every calculation. A generator expression such as (row["minutes"] for row in records) produces those values as they are requested; sum(...) consumes them. It resembles a list comprehension but uses parentheses and need not first construct a list. An ordinary loop is an equally valid way to express the calculation.

worked.code:
import json
text = '[{"game": "Halo", "minutes": 12}]'
records = json.loads(text)
print(sum(row["minutes"] for row in records))
trace: Parse text into a list of dictionaries.
Each record has a minutes value; the generator provides it to sum.
The calculation knows nothing about the source filename, so it is easy to test with a tiny fixture.

plain.title: Files, briefly
plain.text: Programs read and write files with open(). Use it inside a with block, which closes the file for you even if something goes wrong. In Forge's browser exercises you'll usually get the file's text as a string, so you can focus on processing. The local labs use real files.

with open("scores.json") as f:
    text = f.read()
# the file is closed here automatically

plain.title: JSON: data as text
plain.text: JSON is the most common format for sending data between programs and APIs. It looks like Python dictionaries and lists, but it is text. json.loads(text) turns it into Python objects; json.dumps(obj) turns objects back into text.
plain.code:
import json
data = json.loads('{"hp": 5, "tags": ["rpg"]}')
print(data["hp"] + 1)              # 6
print(json.dumps({"ok": True}))     # {"ok": true}

plain.title: CSV: spreadsheets as text
plain.text: CSV is how spreadsheets travel. It looks easy to parse with split(','), but values can contain commas inside quotes. The csv module handles that correctly. DictReader gives each row as a dictionary keyed by the header.
plain.code:
import csv, io
text = "item,price\n\"Potion, large\",3\n"
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text)):
    print(row["item"], float(row["price"]))   # Potion, large 3.0

plain.title: Paths are structured
plain.text: pathlib.Path understands file paths, so you don't have to slice strings yourself. It knows the file name (.name), the extension (.suffix), and the name without it (.stem).
plain.code:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path("saves/slot1.json")
print(p.name, p.suffix, p.stem)   # slot1.json .json slot1

plain.title: Reading and writing a real file
plain.text:
The browser has a small private file system, so real file code works here too. Mode "w" creates or replaces a file, "a" adds to the end, and "r" (the default) reads. Looping over a file gives one line at a time, and each line keeps its newline, so strip it.

The with block closes the file for you, even if an error happens inside it. Always use with.
plain.code:
import os, tempfile
path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "scores.txt")
with open(path, "w") as f:
    f.write("Ada,10\n")
    f.write("Bo,25\n")
with open(path) as f:
    for line in f:
        name, score = line.strip().split(",")
        print(name, int(score))

sections.title: Separate plan from action
sections.text: A file automation tool should first calculate a list of proposed operations. A preview shows source and destination so the user can inspect the plan. The execution layer receives an approved plan; it should not invent additional changes. In this course, start with a folder of disposable sample files and preserve the originals.

sections.title: Collisions are more than duplicate input
sections.text: Two differently spelled files can normalize to the same target. A target might also already exist without appearing in the plan. Case sensitivity differs between filesystems, so a rename that looks safe on one machine may collide on another. Your lab should state its target-platform assumptions and reject a conflicting plan before applying any part of it.

sections.title: Idempotence and reruns
sections.text: An idempotent transformation has the same result after applying it twice. Stripping and lowercasing a tag is often idempotent. A tool that appends a timestamp every run is not. Test reruns explicitly: a second normalization pass should produce no extra changes. Idempotence is a useful property, not a substitute for testing all side effects.

sections.title: A helpful audit
sections.text: An audit counts intended changes and conflict groups, not just raw rows. Keep counts and reasons so someone can understand why execution is blocked. A command-line dry run should make the planned actions clear without writing. When you later add writes, log the operation outcome and make failure behavior explicit rather than assuming every rename succeeds.

plain.title: Automation that doesn't hurt you
plain.text: Automation scripts touch real files and data, so mistakes are expensive. Professionals split every automated change into two steps: plan (work out exactly what would change, and show it) and apply (do it). A plan can be reviewed, tested, and run safely as many times as you like.
plain.code:
def rename_plan(names):
    plan = []
    for old in names:
        new = old.lower().replace(" ", "_")
        if new != old:                 # skip no-op changes
            plan.append([old, new])
    return plan                       # nothing has been renamed yet

plain.title: Collisions and reruns
plain.text: Two different inputs can produce the same output ('My Save' and 'my_save' both become 'my_save'). A good plan detects that before it overwrites something. And a good script is idempotent: running it twice gives the same result as running it once, so a crash halfway through is easy to recover from.

plain.title: Dry runs
plain.text: Most professional command-line tools have a --dry-run flag that prints the plan without applying it. You'll build one in week 13. Get in the habit now: never write code that changes things without a way to preview what it will do.

goals: Explain linear time versus nested repeated work.

sections.title: What complexity measures
sections.text: Big-O describes how work or extra storage grows as input size n grows. It is not a precise stopwatch prediction. A single scan is O(n); a pair of nested scans over n items is often O(n²). Sorting is generally O(n log n). Dictionary and set membership are average O(1) in ordinary use, so a scan with membership checks is average O(n). State assumptions rather than promising constant speed for every implementation.

sections.title: Search and early returns
sections.text: Linear search checks items in order and can stop on the first match. Best case may inspect one item; worst case may inspect all n. Returning -1 is a specific contract, not a universal missing-value rule. An empty input is a useful case because the loop never executes and must still return the correct absent result.

sections.title: Remember previous work
sections.text: A set answers have I seen this value? A dictionary can also retain where it appeared. In two-sum, target - current is the needed complement. Check earlier values before storing the current index so you cannot pair an item with itself. With duplicate values, decide which earlier index the spec requires.

sections.title: Communicate before optimizing
sections.text: Start by restating inputs, outputs, and edge cases. Describe a simple correct approach, then identify repeated work. Explain why the chosen collection removes that work. Walk through a short example and discuss time and space. Memorizing a particular solution is weaker preparation than explaining why its invariant holds.

plain.title: What interviewers are actually checking
plain.text:
Entry-level technical interviews mostly test whether you can: understand a problem and ask about edge cases, get to a correct solution, explain your thinking while you work, and reason about efficiency. Fancy tricks matter much less than clear thinking out loud.

A reliable script: restate the problem, try a small example by hand, describe a simple approach, code it, test it on your example and an edge case, then discuss how fast it is and whether it can be improved.

plain.title: Big O in plain English
plain.text: Big O describes how the work grows as the input grows. Looking at every item once is O(n): double the input, double the work. Comparing every item with every other item is O(n²): double the input, four times the work. Looking something up in a dictionary or set is about O(1): it stays fast no matter how big it gets.

plain.title: The hash-map trick
plain.text: Many interview problems ask 'is there an earlier item that pairs with this one?' Instead of searching backward every time (slow), remember what you've seen in a dictionary (fast). That turns an O(n²) solution into O(n), and it's the single most useful interview idea.

watch.label: CS50x Week 3 (Algorithms): searching, sorting, and Big O

goals: Maintain an invariant while moving pointers.
Use a stack for unfinished nested structure.
Trace a binary-search interval without skipping values.

sections.title: Two pointers
sections.text: Two indices can inspect a sequence from opposite ends or maintain a window. For a palindrome, outer pairs already checked must match, and each step moves inward. The loop ends when pointers meet or cross. A simple drawing of left and right often reveals an off-by-one bug more quickly than repeated code edits.

sections.title: Stacks and nesting
sections.text: A stack removes the most recently added item first. A list with append and pop implements this behavior. Parenthesis validation pushes an opener and pops on a matching closer. A closer with an empty stack fails immediately; unmatched openers fail at the end. Extending to several bracket types requires checking the opener type, not just the count.

sections.title: Sliding windows
sections.text: A fixed-size window sum can move by subtracting the outgoing value and adding the incoming one. Initialize the best result from a real window, not 0, or all-negative data may be wrong. If the window size is invalid, return the contract’s chosen result before taking a slice. Later you will extend this to a variable-size window.

sections.title: Binary search
sections.text: Binary search requires an ordered domain. For an inclusive interval [left, right], search while left <= right. After inspecting mid, discard it and the impossible side using mid + 1 or mid - 1. Every unsuccessful step must shrink the interval. Returning an index after sorting an originally unsorted list would refer to a different order; do not quietly change the meaning of an index.

trace: For level, compare l/l, then e/e. The pointers meet at v.
For ab, the first comparison fails immediately.
The already-checked outer region remains valid throughout the scan.

questions: What fact is true before and after every pointer step?

plain.title: Patterns, not memorized answers
plain.text: Most easy and medium interview problems are variations on a handful of patterns. Learn to recognize the pattern from the problem's shape, then adapt it. This week covers four of the most common.

plain.title: Two pointers
plain.text: Put one index at each end (or both at the start) and move them toward each other based on a rule. This checks palindromes, merges sorted lists, and finds pairs in sorted data in one pass.

plain.title: Stacks
plain.text: A stack is last-in, first-out, like a pile of plates. In Python, use a list with .append() and .pop(). Stacks are perfect for anything nested: brackets, undo history, or walking back through a path.

plain.title: Sliding window and binary search
plain.text: A sliding window keeps a running result for a range of consecutive items and slides it one step at a time instead of recomputing from scratch. Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted range, finding an item in O(log n). For binary search, draw the low and high indexes on paper for every step: almost every bug is an off-by-one in those two lines.

sections.title: Objects and methods
sections.text: A class defines a type; an instance is a particular object of that type. __init__ initializes each instance. self refers to the instance whose method is being called. Put per-player values on self so two players do not accidentally share state. A class-level mutable collection is shared and can create subtle bugs if you intended separate inventories.

sections.title: Functions or classes?
sections.text: Use a function for a straightforward transformation. A class helps when data and operations belong together over time, such as a wallet or game state. Do not create a class merely to hold unrelated utility functions. Composition lets one object use another for storage or formatting while keeping responsibilities distinct.

sections.title: Interfaces and invariants
sections.text: An interface is the behavior callers can rely on: arguments, results, errors, and side effects. A wallet may promise balance never becomes negative. Test that invariant after every transaction, especially rejected ones. Return values and exceptions should follow documented policies so callers do not have to inspect implementation details.

sections.title: Readable pipelines
sections.text: A small pipeline might normalize input, filter records, rank candidates, then format output. Give each step a name that describes its result. A list comprehension is appropriate when it remains readable; a short loop is often clearer when there are several conditions or validation steps. Prioritize code a teammate can inspect and change safely.

units.title: Make code maintainable

plain.title: Classes bundle data with behavior
plain.text: A class is a blueprint for objects that hold their own data (attributes) and know how to act on it (methods). __init__ runs when you create an object and sets its starting state on self. Every method receives the object itself as self, and that's how it reads and changes the object's data.
plain.code:
class Wallet:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.balance = balance          # state lives on self

    def spend(self, amount):
        if amount > self.balance:       # protect the invariant
            return False
        self.balance -= amount
        return True

w = Wallet(10)
w.spend(4)
print(w.balance)    # 6

plain.title: When to use a class
plain.text: Use a plain function when you just transform input into output. Use a class when something has state that changes over time and rules that protect it, like a wallet that can never go negative. Don't make classes just because it feels more professional; simpler is better.

plain.title: Reading self
plain.text:
self trips up nearly everyone at first. It just means 'the object this method was called on'. When you write w.spend(4), Python really runs Wallet.spend(w, 4), so inside the method, self is w.

That's how two wallets can share the same code and still keep separate balances: each method call works on its own object.

plain.title: Inheritance: a kind of
plain.text:
class Boss(Enemy) means a Boss is a kind of Enemy. It gets every method for free, and can override the ones that differ. super() calls the parent's version, so shared rules stay in one place.

Use it only for a real 'is a kind of' relationship. If you only want to reuse some code, a helper function or an object held in an attribute is usually simpler. That's week 18's composition.

plain.title: Special methods
plain.text:
Methods with double underscores plug your class into Python's own syntax. __str__ controls what print shows. __eq__ controls ==. __len__ makes len() work.

Without __eq__, two objects with identical data are not equal, because == falls back to asking whether they're the same object.

sections.title: Start with acceptance examples

sections.title: A record boundary
sections.text: Normalize each record once before storing or combining it. Use a stable key such as a stripped lowercase title if that is your chosen identity policy. Preserve a display title separately if the user needs original capitalization. A missing value, explicit null, and empty string can represent different situations; make the policy visible. A set comprehension such as {tag.strip().lower() for tag in tags if tag.strip()} builds unique normalized values; sorted(...) then gives deterministic output. Dictionary comprehensions use {key: value for ...} to produce mappings.

sections.title: Composition into a tool
sections.text: A CLI can have import, list, search, and export commands. The core accepts ordinary Python data and returns ordinary results. The outer layer parses arguments and opens files. main() owns presentation and exit codes. A module imported in tests should not prompt for input or overwrite files.

plain.title: From exercises to a tool
plain.text:
Real tools are small functions connected together: read input, clean it, process it, and write output. Keep the pieces separate. The functions that do the work should take plain values and return plain values (easy to test), and a thin outer layer handles files and printing.

Write down what 'done' means before you start: a couple of example inputs with their exact expected outputs. Those examples become your tests.

plain.title: Tests you write yourself
plain.text: A test calls your function with a known input and checks the result. Python's built-in unittest module runs a folder of these automatically. In the local labs you'll write them. Every bug you fix should leave behind a test that would have caught it.

plain.title: What makes a good test
plain.text:
A test is only worth something if it could fail. Before you write one, ask: what bug would this catch? Then choose inputs that separate the right answer from likely wrong ones.

For most functions that means a normal case, an empty case, the exact boundaries, and something invalid. A suite that only tries one friendly input feels safe and proves almost nothing.

The new 'Write tests that catch bugs' quests give you broken code and ask you to write the tests that expose it.
plain.code:
def clamp(x, low, high):
    return max(low, min(x, high))

assert clamp(5, 0, 10) == 5     # normal
assert clamp(-1, 0, 10) == 0    # below
assert clamp(11, 0, 10) == 10   # above
assert clamp(0, 0, 10) == 0     # exact edge
print("all passed")

plain.title: Modules and the main guard
plain.text:
Any .py file can be imported by another. Keep logic in functions in one file (core.py) and put printing and input in another (main.py). That separation is what makes your code testable.

The line if __name__ == "__main__": runs its block only when the file is run directly, not when it's imported. Your tests can import the file without kicking off the program.

A checkmark cannot certify job readiness; local labs, unseen tasks, and maintainable handoffs reveal skills that a short function check cannot.

plain.title: Proving it to yourself
plain.text:
This week's challenges come with less guidance on purpose. That's the point: confidence comes from finishing something you weren't walked through. If you get stuck, go back to the method from week 1: write the inputs and outputs, work an example by hand, write the simplest correct code, and trace the failing case.

Use the help ladder honestly. A redo bounty later is a better outcome than a fake clear now.

plain.title: When you're stuck on a blank page
plain.text:
A blank page is hard because you're trying to hold the whole program in your head. Don't. Work through these in order:

1. Write one example input and its exact output as a comment.
2. Solve that example by hand, and write down the steps in plain words.
3. Turn each step into a comment.
4. Fill in the code under one comment at a time, running as you go.
5. Only then think about edge cases.

Almost every program is built from patterns you already know: an accumulator, a counter, a dictionary lookup, a filter, a best-so-far. Ask which one fits.

plain.title: Checking your own confidence
plain.text:
Confidence doesn't come from finishing lessons. It comes from evidence. After this week, try this test: open a blank file, close Forge, and rebuild any weeks 1–9 exercise from memory.

If you can do that with a few quick lookups, the foundations are solid and you're ready for week 13. If not, spend a week in the practice grinds and the skill review first. Going back isn't failing; moving on with shaky foundations is what makes weeks 13–24 feel impossible.

goals: Run a script from a terminal and select the right interpreter.

sections.title: Interpreter, environment, and dependencies
sections.text: A terminal runs commands in a current directory. The Python executable launches your script; the interpreter selected in VS Code should be the same environment your terminal commands use. Create .venv with python -m venv .venv. On Windows you can invoke .venv\Scripts\python directly without activating; on macOS/Linux use .venv/bin/python. Install project dependencies through that interpreter using -m pip. Record dependencies for a clean setup rather than relying on packages installed elsewhere.

sections.title: Git’s three locations
sections.text: Your working tree contains editable files. git add places a snapshot into the staging area. git commit records the staged snapshot, not every subsequent edit. Use git status, git diff, and git diff --staged to inspect each location. Start a branch for a focused change, commit useful checkpoints, and review the diff before sharing. A remote is another repository; pushing a commit is distinct from creating it locally.

sections.title: Entry points and arguments
sections.text: Write main() to parse arguments, call a core function, present results, and return an exit code. if __name__ == "__main__": raises SystemExit(main()) only when launched as a script. argparse can provide --help, value conversion, defaults, and flags. Parse values once at the boundary and pass them as ordinary arguments. Environment variables also arrive as strings and need explicit validation.

sections.title: A small collaboration loop
sections.text: Create a short branch, make one change, run tests, inspect the diff, commit, and open a practice PR in your own repository. Explain the problem, resulting behavior, and test evidence. Exclude .venv, generated outputs, and secrets in .gitignore. If you encounter a conflict, inspect both intended changes rather than deleting markers blindly.

import argparse

parser.add_argument("--count", type=int, default=2)
args = parser.parse_args(["--count", "4"])
print(args.count * 3)

The core expression receives an integer and multiplies it.
The provided list makes the example deterministic; a CLI uses actual command-line arguments.

Thinking a commit automatically uploads code.

units.title: Work like a developer

plain.title: The terminal, in plain English
plain.text:
The terminal is a text way of telling your computer what to do. You'll use a few commands constantly: cd changes folder, ls (or dir) lists files, and python runs a script. Everything you do in a file manager can be done here, and it can be automated, which is why developers use it.

Anything typed after your script's name reaches your program as a list of strings. A program that takes arguments can be used by other programs, not just by you.
plain.code:
cd my_project
python -m venv .venv
python report.py --limit 5 --dry-run

plain.title: Git: save points with notes
plain.text:
Git keeps a history of your project. Think of it as save points in a game, each with a note saying what changed. There are three places a change can be: your working folder (edited), the staging area (chosen for the next save), and the history (saved).

git status shows where everything is. git add chooses, git commit saves, and git diff shows exactly what changed. Run git status often; it's always safe.

The habit that matters: small commits with clear messages, so you can always get back to something that worked.
plain.code:
git status
git add report.py
git commit -m "Add --limit option"
git log --oneline

plain.title: Configuration belongs outside your code
plain.text:
Passwords, API keys, and settings that change between machines shouldn't be in your source code. Read them from the environment instead. Environment values are always text, so "0" and "false" are both truthy strings: compare them, don't just test them.

Never commit a secret. Removing it later doesn't help, because Git remembers everything.
plain.code:
import os
port = int(os.environ.get("APP_PORT", "8000"))
debug = os.environ.get("DEBUG", "").lower() in ("1", "true")
print(port, debug)

sections.title: Arrange, act, assert
sections.text: A useful test sets up a small input, performs one operation, and checks the promised result. Name the behavior, not the line number. Include normal, empty, invalid, and boundary examples where applicable. A test that copies the implementation’s calculation can reproduce the same bug; choose expected outputs from the specification or a hand-worked example.

sections.title: Local testing tools
sections.text: unittest is built into Python; the lab kits use it without extra dependencies. pytest discovers test_*.py files and ordinary test functions with assertions. Locally install pytest into .venv and run python -m pytest. Use pytest.raises for errors and parametrize for several examples of the same behavior. Keep generated files and network calls out of unit tests unless they are the behavior under test.

sections.title: Fakes and interfaces
sections.text: Pass a fetcher, clock, or storage object to code that depends on it. Tests can substitute a fake with known output and inspect whether it was called. Prefer a small fake matching the interface over mocking deep internal implementation details. Type hints document expected shapes but do not validate runtime input; validate untrusted values separately.

sections.title: A debugging workflow
sections.text: Capture the failure, reproduce it with the smallest input, inspect variables, state a hypothesis, and test one change. After correcting it, keep a regression test. A debugger lets you pause at a breakpoint, step into a function, and inspect local values. Logs help explain longer-lived behavior; they should complement a reproducible case rather than replace it.

plain.title: Debugging is a method, not a talent
plain.text:
Good debuggers aren't smarter. They guess less. The loop is always the same:

1. Reproduce it with the smallest input that fails.
2. Say what you expected and what actually happened.
3. Form one guess about why.
4. Test that guess with a print or a debugger, not by changing code at random.
5. Fix it, then keep a test so it can't come back.

If you've changed three things and don't know which one helped, go back. A breakpoint() line pauses your program so you can look at every variable.

plain.title: pytest in five minutes
plain.text:
pytest finds functions named test_something in files named test_*.py and runs them. A plain assert is all you need. When one fails, pytest shows you both values.

Write the failing test first when you fix a bug. Watching it fail proves the test really checks the bug; watching it pass proves the fix works. Forge's browser checks work like this, and your local labs use real pytest.

plain.title: Custom exceptions
plain.text: A custom exception is a one-line class that names a problem in your program's own language. Callers can then catch exactly that problem and let everything else through. Catching plain Exception hides real bugs, so catch the narrowest thing you have a plan for.

goals: Use a bounded regex rather than a vague pattern.

sections.title: Validation is a contract
sections.text: A record can parse as JSON and still be invalid for your application. Validate required keys, types, allowed ranges, and normalization rules. In Python bool is a subclass of int, so type(value) is int can be useful when booleans must not count as quantities. Missing fields and explicit null need deliberate policies.

sections.title: Patterns and parsing
sections.text: re.fullmatch checks an entire value against a pattern. Prefer ASCII ranges when your format requires ASCII digits or letters. A raw string such as r"[0-9]{4}" keeps backslashes for the regex engine. Regex is good for a defined text grammar; calendar validity and general HTML need appropriate parsers instead.

sections.title: Dates and money
sections.text: Use date.fromisoformat for an agreed calendar format, and subtract dates to obtain timedeltas. A timestamp needs a timezone policy; use aware UTC values internally when measuring instants. Use integer cents or Decimal constructed from text for currency. Decide how to reject or round extra precision rather than inheriting binary-float artifacts.

sections.title: Rejected data is still information
sections.text: Keep a row index and a clear reason when validation fails. Count every input in accepted, rejected, or duplicate categories so the report reconciles. Preserve the original source for repair. Error output should help someone fix a bad row without exposing unrelated private data.

worked.code:
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
print((date(2024, 3, 1) - date(2024, 2, 28)).days)
print(int((Decimal("0.10") + Decimal("0.20")) * 100))
trace: The date calculation handles the leap day rather than guessing month lengths.
The currency calculation parses decimal strings exactly before converting to cents.
Neither task needs manual string arithmetic.

mistakes: Using a permissive pattern that accepts extra text.
Constructing Decimal from a binary float.
Discarding rejected records without a count or reason.
questions: What is your invalid-record policy?
Is the value a date or an instant?
Why should True not count as one minute in this schema?

plain.title: Regular expressions without the fear
plain.text:
A regular expression describes a pattern of text. \d is a digit, \w a letter, digit or underscore, + means one or more, and { } gives an exact count. Parentheses capture part of a match.

There are three functions to remember. re.fullmatch checks a whole string, which is what you want for validation. re.findall gets every match. re.sub replaces them.

Keep patterns short. If one is hard to read, split the job into steps or use ordinary string methods.
plain.code:
import re
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d{3}", "123")))     # True
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r"\d{3}", "1234")))    # False
print(re.findall(r"#(\w+)", "#a and #b"))       # ['a', 'b']
print(re.sub(r"\d", "*", "pin 1234"))           # pin ****

plain.title: Dates and times
plain.text:
Dates are not text. Text can't tell you the day after February 28th, or how many days are in a month. Convert to date objects as soon as data arrives, do your work, and convert back when you need to show it.

The ISO format YYYY-MM-DD is worth using everywhere: it's unambiguous and sorts correctly even as text.
plain.code:
from datetime import date, timedelta
start = date.fromisoformat("2024-02-28")
print(start + timedelta(days=2))        # 2024-03-01: a leap year
print((date(2024, 12, 25) - start).days)
print(start.strftime("%b %d, %Y"))

plain.title: Why money isn't a float
plain.text:
Floats are stored in binary, which can't represent 0.1 exactly, just as a decimal can't write 1/3 exactly. The errors are tiny, but they add up, and exact comparisons fail.

For money, use Decimal built from text, or store whole cents as integers.
plain.code:
from decimal import Decimal
print(0.1 + 0.2)                        # 0.30000000000000004
print(Decimal("0.10") + Decimal("0.20"))  # 0.30

goals: Run SELECT, filtering, sorting, and grouping.
Join related tables and preserve missing matches when appropriate.

sections.title: Rows, keys, and queries
sections.text: A relational table has named columns and rows. A primary key identifies a row; a foreign key relates it to another table. SELECT chooses columns and WHERE restricts input rows. ORDER BY is required when the caller expects a particular order. SQLite supports local file databases and in-memory databases; a connection is a resource that should be closed.

sections.title: Group and join
sections.text: GROUP BY collects rows for aggregates such as SUM and COUNT. HAVING restricts resulting groups. An INNER JOIN returns matching relationships; a LEFT JOIN preserves each left row, including those without a match. Missing right values are NULL. COALESCE can provide an explicit replacement. Join multiplicity matters: joining several child records produces several rows before aggregation.

sections.title: Parameters and transaction boundaries
sections.text: Use ? placeholders and a separate tuple of values rather than string interpolation. The one-value tuple is (value,), including the comma. Parameters represent values, not arbitrary table names. A transaction groups updates that must either all persist or all roll back. Enforce important consistency rules through constraints as well as application validation.

sections.title: Persistence and performance
sections.text: An in-memory exercise checks query logic, while a file database survives a new process. Commit intended changes and test persistence. An index can improve lookups at the cost of storage and write work; inspect query behavior rather than indexing every column. A schema migration changes stored structure and needs a plan for existing records.

worked.code:
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE scores(name TEXT, points INTEGER)")
con.executemany("INSERT INTO scores VALUES (?, ?)", [("A", 3), ("B", 8)])
rows = con.execute("SELECT name FROM scores WHERE points >= ? ORDER BY name", (5,)).fetchall()
print(rows)
con.close()
trace: The schema gives names and points separate columns.
Values are inserted and filtered using bound parameters.
fetchall returns a list of row tuples, even when one selected column is present.

Assuming row order without ORDER BY.
Using INNER JOIN when zero-session games must remain in the report.
questions: What changes when a join matches several child rows?
Why is (value,) different from (value)?
Which updates must commit together?

units.title: Store and query data

plain.title: What a database gives you
plain.text:
A file holds data. A database also keeps it consistent while many things read and change it, and answers questions quickly. Data lives in tables: rows are records and columns are fields. A primary key identifies a row, and a foreign key points to a row in another table.

SQL says what you want, not how to get it. Read a query in this order: FROM picks the table, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY forms groups, SELECT chooses columns, ORDER BY sorts.
plain.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE scores (name TEXT, score INTEGER)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO scores VALUES (?, ?)", [("Ada", 9), ("Bo", 4)])
for row in db.execute("SELECT name FROM scores WHERE score > 5"):
    print(row)

plain.title: Joins
plain.text:
Related data is split across tables so each fact lives in one place. A join puts it back together for a query. An inner JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table, with NULL where nothing matched.

If rows go missing from your report, you probably wanted LEFT JOIN. If your counts are too big, a join has probably duplicated rows.

plain.title: Parameters and transactions
plain.text:
Two rules keep database code safe. First, never build SQL with an f-string. Use ? placeholders, so values can't be mistaken for commands. That's the whole defense against SQL injection.

Second, group changes that belong together in a transaction. commit() makes them permanent. rollback() undoes them. A transfer that takes money out but crashes before putting it in must not half-happen.
plain.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE p (name TEXT)")
name = "O'Neil"
db.execute("INSERT INTO p VALUES (?)", (name,))
print(db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM p WHERE name = ?", (name,)).fetchone())

sections.title: The request/response boundary
sections.text: An HTTP request specifies a method, URL, headers, and sometimes a body. The response has a status, headers, and body. GET commonly retrieves a resource; POST commonly creates or processes one. A successful transport response does not prove the data has the schema you expect. Check the service’s contract before processing its JSON.

sections.title: A reliable local client
sections.text: Use a maintained client such as Requests locally. Set timeouts and handle connection and HTTP errors. Requests timeout behavior is not a whole-operation stopwatch; it bounds waiting for relevant network activity. Decode JSON only when appropriate and validate the result. Build query parameters through the library rather than concatenating a user string containing &, spaces, or ?.

sections.title: Pagination and retries
sections.text: An API may return a page and a next token. Bound the page count and detect a repeated token. Deduplicate through stable ids when the service can return overlaps. Retry only when the operation and error justify it, with a limit and backoff. A retryable read differs from a potentially duplicate write. Respect the service’s published rate-limit policy.

sections.title: Offline tests before live calls
sections.text: A fake response lets tests cover 200, missing resource, malformed data, timeout, and a failing middle page without depending on live internet. The browser challenges operate on such fixtures. The local lab adds the real HTTP adapter. This keeps correctness checks reproducible and avoids mistaking a service outage for your algorithm’s bug.

units.title: Talk to services
units.prerequisites: Weeks 1–16, especially store and query data

plain.title: HTTP is a conversation
plain.text:
A client sends a request, and a server sends back a response. A request has a method (GET to read, POST to create, PUT or PATCH to change, DELETE to remove), a URL, headers, and sometimes a body. A response has a status code, headers, and a body, which is usually JSON.

The first digit of the status tells you who to blame. 2xx worked. 3xx look elsewhere. 4xx your request was wrong. 5xx the server failed.
plain.code:
import json
response_status = 200
response_body = '{"title": "Halo", "year": 2001}'
if 200 <= response_status <= 299:
    game = json.loads(response_body)
    print(game["title"])

plain.title: Networks fail, so plan for it
plain.text:
Local code usually works or doesn't. Network calls can be slow, fail halfway, or succeed while you never hear back. So always set a timeout, retry only what might work next time (429 and 5xx, not 404), wait longer between tries, and limit how many tries you make.

Forge can't reach real services from its exercises, so they use recorded responses. Your local labs make real calls.

goals: Avoid shared mutable defaults.
Use instances, helpers, and modules with clear boundaries.
Distinguish a generator from a stored list.

sections.title: Functions and scope
sections.text: Parameters and local names belong to a function call. Defaults are created when a function is defined, so a default list may persist across calls. Use a None sentinel and construct fresh mutable state when needed. Keyword arguments improve clarity at call sites, and a docstring should describe meaning, errors, and side effects rather than merely repeat the function name.

sections.title: Organize responsibilities
sections.text: Keep parsing, domain rules, storage, and presentation distinct. Small modules can expose a few documented functions or classes. Importing a module should not automatically run the application. Composition lets a service use a repository object; avoid deep inheritance trees when a small explicit dependency is enough. A dataclass can express a simple record, but does not replace input validation.

sections.title: Iterables and generators
sections.text: A for loop can consume a list, range, file iterator, or generator. A generator uses yield to provide one value and pause until the next request. It can avoid retaining an entire intermediate collection. Once exhausted it does not restart itself; create a new iterator if needed. Streaming a file line by line can reduce memory while still requiring state for any aggregate you maintain.

sections.title: Configuration and contracts
sections.text: Merge defaults, file settings, and explicit options according to a documented precedence. Preserve supplied zero and False values rather than using truthy fallbacks. Validate once after the merge. Keep a typed settings object separate from the loader so tests can provide configuration directly.

trace: Each omitted items argument becomes a fresh list inside the call.
Concatenation returns a new list rather than changing a supplied list.
The second call has no hidden dependency on the first call’s history.

mistakes: Putting [] or {} in a default argument unintentionally.
Using a generator twice and expecting the second pass to replay it.
Making a class merely to group unrelated functions.

Which module owns storage?
What does your public function promise about mutation?

units.title: Design maintainable Python

plain.title: Mutable defaults
plain.text: Default argument values are created once, when the function is defined, not on each call. So a default list is shared by every call, and it keeps growing. The standard fix is a default of None, and a fresh list inside.
plain.code:
def add(item, items=None):
    if items is None:
        items = []
    items.append(item)
    return items

print(add("a"))
print(add("b"))   # ['b'], not ['a', 'b']

plain.title: Generators
plain.text: A function with yield doesn't run straight through. Each next() runs it up to the next yield, then pauses it with its variables intact. Nothing happens until someone asks for a value, which means a generator can read a huge file line by line without loading it all.

plain.title: Decorators
plain.text:
A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new one that adds behavior. Writing @timer above a def is shorthand for add = timer(add).

Functions are values, which is why this works. Decorators are everywhere in real Python: @app.route in web frameworks, @pytest.fixture in tests, @property in classes.

plain.title: Dataclasses and properties
plain.text: A dataclass is a class that mainly holds data. You list the fields and Python writes __init__, __eq__ and a useful printout for you. A @property is a method you read like an attribute, so a computed value can never go stale.

plain.title: Context managers
plain.text: with isn't only for files. Any object with __enter__ and __exit__ works. Python guarantees __exit__ runs however the block ends, even on an error. That makes it the right tool for anything that must be cleaned up: files, database connections, locks.

goals: Recognize a recursive base case.
Use BFS for an unweighted shortest path.
Explain linked traversal and a priority queue.

sections.title: Data structure vocabulary
sections.text: An array-like sequence supports position-based access; a linked structure follows references. A graph consists of vertices and edges, represented here by a dictionary of neighbor lists. A tree is a special connected acyclic structure; recursive traversal can be natural but still requires a stopping case. Know the operations and costs rather than memorizing a diagram.

sections.title: Recursion and traversal
sections.text: A recursive solution has a base case and a smaller subproblem. Trace one call chain and its returns. Python has a finite recursion depth, so deep input may require a stack-based version. A linked-list traversal follows next until None; reversing a chain requires preserving the next reference before overwriting it.

sections.title: Queues and graph search
sections.text: BFS uses a first-in, first-out queue and visits an unweighted graph by increasing path length. collections.deque supports efficient popleft. Mark a node seen when enqueuing it so cycles do not cause repeated work. With adjacency lists the usual traversal work is O(V + E), where V is visited vertices and E is examined edges. Weighted shortest routes need a different algorithm.

sections.title: Priority and pattern selection
sections.text: A heap makes the smallest priority available without fully sorting on every insertion. Include a sequence number to preserve a tie order. Sorting once may be simpler for a static batch; a heap becomes useful when work arrives dynamically. For interviews, learn to explain why a stack, queue, map, or heap fits the behavior, and practice unfamiliar variations.

trace: The start node enters the queue with distance 0.
Its neighbor is marked seen and queued at distance 1.
The queue processes the neighbor after all earlier entries; the empty neighbor list ends the traversal.

units.title: Broaden your problem-solving toolkit

plain.title: How to think recursively
plain.text:
Recursion is a function calling itself on a smaller problem. Every recursive function has two parts. The base case is the smallest input, answered directly. The recursive case shrinks the problem and uses the answer.

Don't try to trace every call in your head. Trust the rule: assume the smaller call already works, then ask how to use it. Trace by hand only when debugging, and start with the smallest input.

Python stops at about 1,000 nested calls. If you see RecursionError, your base case is probably wrong or never reached.
plain.code:
def total(nums):
    if not nums:              # base case: nothing left
        return 0
    return nums[0] + total(nums[1:])   # first item + the rest

print(total([1, 2, 3]))   # 1 + (2 + (3 + 0))

plain.title: Trees and graphs
plain.text:
A tree is data where each item has children and there are no loops, like folders or a comment thread. Tree code is usually recursive: solve the children, then combine.

A graph is items joined by connections, like cities and roads. It can have loops, so you must remember where you've been. Store it as a dictionary from each node to its neighbors.

Use breadth-first search with a deque to find the shortest route in steps. Use depth-first search when you only need to explore everything.

plain.title: Memoization: remember the answers
plain.text:
Some recursive functions solve the same smaller problem again and again. fib(30) calls itself over a million times. Save each answer the first time and the work becomes linear. That's memoization, and it's the core idea of dynamic programming.

functools.lru_cache does it with one line. Ask: are the same inputs coming up repeatedly? If so, cache them.

plain.title: Heaps: always know the smallest
plain.text: A heap keeps its smallest item at the front without fully sorting. Adding and removing are O(log n), so it's perfect when items keep arriving and you always need the next most important one, like a task queue.
plain.code:
import heapq
tasks = []
heapq.heappush(tasks, (2, "write"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (1, "plan"))
heapq.heappush(tasks, (3, "ship"))
while tasks:
    print(heapq.heappop(tasks))

units.title: Build a small backend
units.prerequisites: Weeks 1–19, especially broaden your problem-solving toolkit

plain.title: What a backend actually does
plain.text:
A backend is a program that waits for requests. For each one it does the same few things: match the URL to a handler, check who's asking, validate the input, do the work (usually with a database), and return a status and JSON.

Frameworks like Flask and FastAPI handle the routing. The rest is ordinary Python, which is why it pays to keep your rules in plain functions you can test without a server.

plain.title: Authentication and authorization
plain.text:
They sound alike but they're different. Authentication asks who you are. Authorization asks what you're allowed to do. Checking only the first is a classic security bug: any logged-in user could edit anyone's data.

Check permission on the server, for every request. Never rely on the interface hiding a button. And don't invent your own password storage or tokens; real projects use tested libraries.

plain.title: Status codes are part of the contract
plain.text:
Clients decide what to do based on your status codes, so be exact. 200 for success, 201 when something was created, 204 for success with nothing to return. 400 for bad input, 401 for not logged in, 403 for not allowed, 404 for not found, 409 for a conflict. 500 means your code broke, so never use it on purpose.

Write down what each endpoint accepts and returns before you build it. That written contract is what other people build against.

sections.title: Observability with a purpose
sections.text: A useful log explains an event, relevant counters, and context such as a run id. Use severity to distinguish ordinary progress from partial rejection or failure. sections.title: Idempotent imports
sections.text: Stable ids and a documented upsert policy prevent reruns from duplicating data. A unique database constraint reinforces the rule. Decide whether a repeated id replaces, merges, or rejects the record. Test both repeats within one batch and re-importing the entire file. A partial failure must not leave a misleading success summary.

sections.text: Accept only the filename forms your tool needs. sections.title: Reconciliation and recovery
sections.text: A batch report should account for every input record. Separate invalid rows from extra valid duplicate ids. Keep original input and a rejection report for repair. Transactions can ensure related database changes are coherent, while a retry policy must avoid duplicating already-applied work. Demonstrate reruns and a forced failure rather than assuming recovery works.

units.title: Make automation dependable
units.prerequisites: Weeks 1–20, especially build a small backend

plain.title: Scripts that run while you sleep
plain.text:
A script you run once can be sloppy. One that runs every night can't, because nobody's watching. Three properties matter. It must be idempotent, meaning running it twice gives the same result as once. It must be observable, so logs say what happened and what was skipped. And it must fail loudly when it can't do its job.

The worst outcome isn't a crash. It's a job that quietly does the wrong thing for three weeks.
plain.code:
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s", force=True)
log = logging.getLogger("import")
rows = ["1", "x", "3"]
good = []
for i, row in enumerate(rows):
    try:
        good.append(int(row))
    except ValueError:
        log.warning("skipped row %d: %r", i, row)
log.info("imported %d, skipped %d", len(good), len(rows) - len(good))

plain.title: Never trust a filename
plain.text:
Any value from outside your program is untrusted, and that includes filenames. A name like ../../secrets.txt escapes the folder you meant to write in. Check the name at the boundary, before using it.

The same habit applies everywhere: validate at the edge of your program, and let the inside assume clean data.

units.title: Maintain and collaborate

plain.title: Reading code you didn't write
plain.text:
Most professional work is changing existing code, not writing new code. Don't read it top to bottom. Start from what you need to change, find where that behavior happens, and trace outward. Run it. Add a print. Read its tests, which show what it's supposed to do.

Before you change anything, get the tests passing, so you know what you broke. Make the smallest change that works. Don't tidy unrelated code in the same change, because it makes your work harder to review and easier to get wrong.

plain.title: Changing things without breaking them
plain.text:
Other code depends on yours, in ways you can't see. A rename that looks harmless can break callers and old saved data. So add before you remove: accept both the old and new shape for a while, move everyone over, and delete the old path later.

Type hints help here. They document what a function expects, and tools like mypy can find callers you'd have broken.

plain.title: Pull requests and code review
plain.text:
A pull request proposes a change and shows the difference. Good ones are small, say why the change is needed, and explain how it was tested.

When reviewing, look for what would break, what's missing, and whether a test proves it works. Comment on the code, not the person. When you receive a review, a comment is information about the code. It's the fastest way to learn how a team thinks.

units.title: Ship and verify your work

plain.title: Done means someone else can run it
plain.text:
Software isn't finished when it works on your machine. It's finished when a stranger can install and run it. Test that literally: clone your repo into a new folder, create a fresh .venv, and follow your own README word for word. You'll find what you forgot.

A good README answers four questions: what is this, how do I run it, how do I test it, and what are its limits? Honest limits build more trust than big claims.
