git clone https://example.com/you/project.git
cd project
python -m venv .venv
pip install -r requirements.txt
pytest

plain.title: Let a robot run the checks
plain.text:
Continuous integration (CI) runs your tests on a clean machine every time you push. It catches 'works on my machine' problems, and it means nobody needs to remember to run the tests. GitHub Actions does this for free on public repos with one small YAML file.

Only automate checks you already run and trust by hand. A red build that everyone ignores is worse than none.

plain.title: Version numbers mean something
plain.text: Semantic versioning uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Patch means a bug fix. Minor adds something without breaking anything. Major means something may break. Pin your dependencies, so what you tested is what gets installed.
plain.code:
parts = "1.10.2".split(".")
major, minor, patch = [int(p) for p in parts]
print(major, minor + 1, 0)

Add role-specific skills when a job description calls for them; frontend, data engineering, and game engines each need further specialization.

units.title: Practice the entry-level transition
units.prerequisites: Weeks 1–23, especially ship and verify your work

plain.title: Solving a problem you've never seen
plain.text:
In an interview or a take-home, the problem will be new. That's expected, and the process doesn't change.

1. Restate it in your own words and ask about edge cases.
2. Work an example by hand.
3. Say a simple approach out loud, even a slow one.
4. Ask which pattern fits: counting, two pointers, a stack, a window, sorting first, BFS, recursion.
5. Code it, talking as you go.
6. Test it with your example and one edge case, then state the complexity.

Interviewers are watching how you think. A working simple answer you can explain beats a clever one you can't.

plain.title: Talking about your projects
plain.text:
You will be asked to explain something you built. Prepare one project using this shape: what the problem was, what you decided and why, something that went wrong and how you found it, and what you'd change now.

Be specific, and be honest about what you used. If you used AI tools, say how, and show that you can explain, change and debug the result yourself. That last part is what employers need, and it's exactly what this course has been training.

plain.title: Are you ready?
plain.text:
There's no certificate that says so. These are better signals. You can start a small program from a blank file. You can read an error and find the cause without guessing. You can write a test that catches a real bug. You can explain your code to someone else. You can take a task you've never seen and make progress.

If most of those are true, start applying. You'll never feel completely finished, and you don't need to. Everyone in this field is still looking things up.

grind.title: Practice grind
grind.text:
Fundamentals stick through many repetitions, not one good attempt. Each drill here is small, aimed at a single idea from that week's chapter. Aim to solve each one with no hints in under 15 minutes.

If a drill takes much longer, that's useful information: go back to the chapter's plain-English section, then try again tomorrow. Speed comes later; accuracy comes first.

bugs.title: Bug hunts
bugs.text:
Each quest gives you code that looks reasonable but is wrong. Your job is to find the bug and fix it with the smallest possible change. This is the skill that matters most now that AI writes so much code: someone has to check it.

The method:
1. Run the checks first, without changing anything. Find the failing case.
2. Trace the code by hand with that exact input, writing down each variable.
3. Stop at the first line where reality differs from what the code should do. Name the bug in one sentence in your notes.
4. Fix only that, then rerun everything.

Resist rewriting the whole function. In a real job, the smallest correct fix is the one that gets approved.
bugs.code:
Common bug families you'll meet:
  off-by-one        > vs >=, range(n) vs range(n + 1)
  wrong default     .get(key, 0) when 0 is a real value
  aliasing          b = a does not copy a list or dict
  early return      return inside a loop's else branch
  order             checking after adding instead of before
  min/max swap      'at least 0' means max(0, x)

sql.title: SQL
sql.text:
SQL is how you ask a database questions. It's what data and BI roles test first, and you'll use it in almost any engineering job. These quests use a small game-library database with three tables: players, games, and sessions (who played what, for how long, and when).

You write a single SELECT statement. Forge runs it against two different datasets and compares your rows (including their order) with the expected answer, so a query has to be truly correct, not just right for one set of data.

A query reads in this order, even though you write SELECT first: FROM (which tables) → JOIN (connect them) → WHERE (filter rows) → GROUP BY (make groups) → HAVING (filter groups) → SELECT (pick columns) → ORDER BY (sort). When a query confuses you, read it in that order.
sql.code:
SELECT g.title, SUM(s.minutes) AS total      -- 6. pick columns
FROM sessions AS s                            -- 1. start here
JOIN games AS g ON g.id = s.game_id           -- 2. connect tables
WHERE s.played_on >= '2026-10-01'             -- 3. filter rows
GROUP BY g.id                                 -- 4. one row per game
HAVING SUM(s.minutes) > 60                    -- 5. filter groups
ORDER BY total DESC, g.title;                 -- 7. sort

interview.title: Interview gauntlet
interview.text:
These are classic entry-level interview problems. Treat each one like a real interview:
1. Restate the problem and ask yourself about edge cases (empty input, duplicates, negatives).
2. Describe a brute-force solution, even if it's slow.
3. Improve it, and say why it's faster.
4. Code it, then test it on a small example out loud.
5. State the time and space complexity.

After you clear one, come back in a few days and solve it from a blank file while talking out loud. Recall under light pressure is what interviews actually measure.

hardware.title: Hardware lab
hardware.text:
These quests are the software side of embedded work: turning raw sensor readings into decisions. They use the same ideas as real sensor projects (barometric pressure and GPS) and run right here in the browser.

To try the real thing, get a Raspberry Pi Pico (or Pico W) starter kit with a breadboard, jumper wires, a push button, an LED, and a BMP280 barometric sensor (roughly $30–50 total). Install the MicroPython firmware, use the Thonny editor, and build in this order:
1. Blink the LED. Then read the button and light the LED while it's pressed.
2. Count button presses using your debounce logic from these quests.
3. Read the BMP280 over I2C and print pressure every second.
4. Convert pressure to altitude with your formula, smooth it with your moving average, and drive the LED as an alarm with hysteresis.

Write every line yourself. If you lose track of time doing this, embedded or test engineering may be your direction.
hardware.code:
# MicroPython on a Pico: blink the onboard LED
from machine import Pin
import time

led = Pin("LED", Pin.OUT)
while True:
    led.toggle()
    time.sleep(0.5)
